articles.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
articles.titleZh: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
articles.summary: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude

blocks.text: 9th November 2026

Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.
Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.
Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such.

Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.
How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.
That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.
How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve
There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it
I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from
There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app
Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?
That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.
The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else
That got me to this point—most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.
I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.
I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate
This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]
Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps
That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.
each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp
That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays
Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for
Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is
At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.
And since I had one spare device, I then said:
add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far
Giving Claude Code ears
I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears.
Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.
Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.
Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

articles.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
articles.titleZh: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
articles.summary: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>

blocks.text: 9th November 2026

Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work—I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today’s coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.
They’re too good at describing the work

The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That’s a lot of information to absorb.
It’s not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop!

It’s very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as “I’m not reading all of that”. It doesn’t matter how accurate or useful the information is, I’m instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!

I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.
I think I’ve found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.
Hide most of it in a details/summary
The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this:

Claude Opus 5.5

The hook

Plugins implement register_agent_reference_types(datasette)...
When rendered, it looks like this:

Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown. You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow.
I’ve started using this for my AI-generated pull requests.
The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what’s going on—the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed.
I’ll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature.

The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary>. I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on—“Claude Opus 5.5 Medium” for example.

My PRs don’t feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details.

I don’t always write the introduction myself—sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time.
Here are some recent examples where I’ve used this pattern, including the opener I used:

datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields—"The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot)

datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page—“Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom.” (plus screenshot)

datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader—"edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn’t edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)."

datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook—"Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook."—pictured above.

llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands—"Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml, so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML."—then copied --help output.
The mnemonic
I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags—is it <details><summary> or <summary><details>?
Here are two tricks that helped me.

First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That’s the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand—the <details> element must then wrap everything else.
An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as “details-summary”.
“details-summary” is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of “summary-details”.
Say “details-summary” out loud just a few times and you’ll never forget the order of the tags again.

(I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this—partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.)

blocks.text: Elon Musk now says Tesla can’t build the Cybertruck and the Cybercab at the same time because there are only so many “smart, dedicated people” to go around. Half the executives he showed off in 2023 as proof of Tesla’s “bench strength” have since left the company.
It’s the most honest explanation yet for how Tesla went from five consumer vehicle programs at the start of 2026 to a single platform, Model 3 and Model Y, by the middle of 2027.
Three explanations in four days

On Friday, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around the middle of next year “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” As we pointed out at the time, Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck line runs at a fraction of its installed capacity because the truck sells a fraction of what Tesla planned.
A day later, replying to a user on X, Musk gave a different reason:
“The biggest thing most people fail to understand is that there are a very limited number of smart, dedicated people! They can only do so many things.”
He added that if Tesla has to “maintain a complex production line, supply chain and allocate engineering for Cybertruck, we can’t use those people” for scaling Cybercab.

By this morning, the explanation had shifted again, to the “opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck.” But the Saturday version is the one that matters. Musk is telling us the bottleneck at Tesla isn’t factory space or money. It’s people.
From five programs to one platform

The Cybertruck is the second casualty this year. In January, Musk announced the end of the Model S and Model X on Tesla’s Q4 earnings call and summed up the reason in one word: “Autonomy.” The Fremont line is being converted to build Optimus robots, and by April, only inventory was left.

We previously explained how this is a terrible idea.

Zach Kirkhorn, CFO, left in August 2023.
Colin Campbell, VP of powertrain engineering, left in 2024 and is now CTO at Redwood Materials.
Drew Baglino, SVP of powertrain and energy engineering, left in April 2024 after 18 years.
Rebecca Tinucci, head of Supercharging, was fired in April 2024 along with most of her team.
David Lau, VP of software engineering, left in April 2025 after 12 years.
Pete Bannon, VP of hardware engineering, left in August 2025 as Tesla shut down its Dojo supercomputer.
Mike Snyder, VP of energy and charging, stepped down last month, according to the Wall Street Journal. Tesla hasn’t confirmed it.
Martin Viecha, who ran investor relations through that event, left in April 2024 as well.

The bigger problem for Tesla’s ability to run vehicle programs is the program-level talent, the people who take a car from prototype to volume production.

In November 2025, Tesla lost the head of its Cybertruck program, Siddhant Awasthi, and the Model Y program manager, Emmanuel Lamacchia, within a day of each other. Lamacchia had led Tesla’s best-selling vehicle for four years.
Then the Cybercab, the program Musk is now pulling people toward, started losing its own leaders:
Victor Nechita, Cybercab vehicle program manager, quit in February 2026, days after the first production unit came off the line.
Mark Lupkey, who ran Cybercab assembly and end-of-line at Giga Texas, left in March.
Michael So, head of Cybercab new product introduction and Giga Texas employee number one, left in April for a nuclear startup.
Jody Kerns, senior manager of Cybercab general assembly, left in October to run R2 general assembly at Rivian.
Add 17-year finance VP Sendil Palani and Thomas Dmytryk, the director who built Tesla’s over-the-air update system and Robotaxi infrastructure, both in March, and you get the picture.
So when Musk says he needs Cybertruck’s people for Cybercab, part of the reason is that Cybercab keeps losing its own.

Each time, the autonomy that justified the change wasn’t there yet.

Both vehicle programs will undoubtedly go down in history as some of the most critical EVs of all time, but that doesn’t guarantee lasting success in a rapidly changing auto landscape.

True Carneyism has never been tried. When Canadian PM Mark Carney traveled to Davos to declare a "rupture" in the old order (and admit that this old order was never that great to begin with) he told us that there was no going back from Trumpism. The only way out of Trumpism was through:
https://www.weforum.org/stories/forum-institutional/davos-2026-special-address-by-mark-carney-prime-minister-of-canada/
This is easy to say, but hard to do. If the old order is over, then we will never again be able to trust America to serve as the world's cop, banker, ISP, IT department and consumer of first resort.
We can't trust Americans to buy the things we make:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/16/k-shaped-recovery/#disenshittification-nations
We can't trust them not to interfere with the interconnections between fiber lines that slither out of the oceans and onto the US landmass:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/26/difficult-multipolarism/#eurostack
We can't trust them not to weaponize the US dollar to undermine sovereign nations' legitimate activities:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/26/i-dont-want/#your-greenback-dollar

And we absolutely can't trust them not to spy on, steal from, and shut down governments, firms and households around the world by cutting off access to US software and cloud services, and by bricking the world's devices, from tractors to smartphones:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

Despite Carney's assertion that this rupture represents a welcome (if too cruel, sudden and painful) departure of the old (never very good) system, no one (not even Carney) is acting like the world has truly changed. Take Carney's answer to the Trump tariffs: retaliatory tariffs. Tariffs have a place in sheltering a nascent domestic industry from better-developed, deeper-pocketed foreign competitors, so a tariff wall between Canada and the US could make sense, if it was paired with the massive domestic investment we'd need to rebuild the manufacturing industry that Brian Mulroney sold out with the Canada-US Free Trade Agreement (and later NAFTA).

But Carney is no Carneyist. When it comes to massive domestic spending, Carney is a bog-standard, austerity-addled Reaganomics guy; a central banker and technocrat whose idea of "industrial policy" is firing tens of thousands of skilled civil servants who thwart his agenda and replacing them with defective (but obedient) chatbots running on US hardware:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/13/vibe-governance/#k-hole

Carney's retaliatory tariffs aren't what you'd do if the old order had "ruptured." They're what you'd do if you hoped that your American cousins would come to their senses, evict their mad king from the White House, tear down the Epstein Memorial Ballroom, and roll back the clock to 2016. Like a lot of liberals, Carney just wants to go back to brunch.

But as any true Carneyist knows, brunch is canceled forever. Brunch ruptured. There's no going back to the old America, and there's no going back to the old American order that had dominated the world since the end of WWII. As November Kelly says, "Trump inherited a poker game rigged in his favor, but he flipped the table over anyway because he resented having to pretend to play."

This is something we're all struggling with, including Americans. The Republicans' midterm wipeout has corporate Democrats hoping that after a few years' tinkering, they can elect a Newsomdroid or give Harris a do-over and win back the trust and reliance of the world and the American people. Even for a true Carneyist who never liked the old order very much (like me), this is a comforting prospect. No one knows what the next world will look like, and no matter how screwed up the old world was, I knew how it worked and how to make it work for me (more or less).

But there is no going back. Trump I didn't have a plan, it only had Trump, whose One Big Idea was issuing Executive Orders. Many of these were meaningless bloviating. Some were illegal and were swiftly suspended or never went into effect. Biden overturned nearly all the remaining EOs (that were both substantive and not totally illegal).

But Trump II had Project 2025. The point of Project 2025 and the ambition of the wreckers who wrote it was to push America through a series of one-way transformations that cannot be undone, and that's what's happened, over two short years. That's the bad news. The good news is that it's much easier to destroy than to build, so Project 2025 hasn't led to the creation of permanent, load-bearing fascist institutions that cannot be shuttered without bringing down large parts of the USA.

Start with values. Trumpism is a denial of democracy and the rule of law. Tens of millions of Americans have been marinated in a belief system that says that the way to win power is to claim all the elections you lose are rigged and that these "stolen elections" are best addressed by staging a coup. These people are in a cult that embraces its leader's naked corruption. They're in a cult whose doctrine treats political triumph of as divine direction to embark on looting sprees. It's a cult whose members mutilate their faces so that they can't ever leave, and the reward for this permanent disfigurement is endless influence-peddling:
https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6136101-ambassador-guilfoyle-wire-request/

Even without ritual scarification to mark them out forever, millions of these people will never come back from this cult indoctrination. They will forever be democracy's enemies, treating the idea of laws, rules and honest service as shucks for the rubes. What's more, these people's neighbors, family members and co-workers will never be able to fully trust them.

Unfortunately, those values aren't just diffused through the population: they are concentrated in the organs of state. DOGE and Federalist Society judicial appointments have created a stay-behind cadre of life-tenured fascists who now dominate America's federal judiciary and permanent civil service, including and especially the nation's law enforcement and national security agencies, from the FBI to the FDA, the NSA to the Bureau of Prisons.

Worse: DOGE also chased away hundreds of thousands of skilled, principled public servants. Those people have retired, retrained, emigrated or exited the workforce. They can't simply be re-hired and restored to their old roles. From finance regulation to the national education system, America has lobotomized itself, swapping people who understand how things work and use that understanding to enforce the laws and safeguard the American people for end-times fascists, caliper-wielding eugenicists, and Ayn Rand LARPers.

Much of the work DOGE's victims did is also gone forever. When DOGE's muskrats killed long-running NIH research projects, they pulled the plug on studies, some of which had run for decades. Many of these experiments are unsalvageable. DOGE didn't just throw away the contributions that cancer patients, people with genetic disorders and other volunteer research subjects gave to science: in halting these research projects, DOGE shredded this selfless sacrifice. Why not? When one NIH official begged his DOGE invaders not to kill long-running, valuable cancer research, the DOGE child laughed and said it didn't matter, because AI was going to cure cancer.

Then there's the NIH's research partners: the elite institutions who buckled so quickly in the face of Trump's antisemitism/DEI witch-hunts. These universities now face the same crisis as the DOGE-gutted civil service, with their best and brightest gone, grad students chased back to their home countries, and the trust of their students and faculty permanently squandered.

It's not just grad students who got chased out of America. Immigrants – documented and undocumented alike – have been terrorized for two years and many of them have fled. ICE got what it wanted: they robbed aging, stagnant America of the dynamism, aspiration and youthful vigor of the most ambitious people from every corner of the globe, people who proved their resourcefulness and bravery by making dangerous crossings. Then they navigated the US immigration system's impenetrable bureaucracy, often working without legal representation, in a language they were just learning, and still managing to clear every bureaucratic hurdle. This alone is a breathtaking demonstration of intelligence, resourcefulness and diligence. Those brilliant, hardworking people aren't coming back: some other country will get the benefit of their life's work and care. Their children will become citizens of other nations.

Now think of the hundreds of billions of dollars that have been transferred from ordinary working people who are still here, to America's oligarchs. Trump's tax cuts, corrupt policy subsidies and no-bid pork contracts have supercharged the wealth (and thus the power) of America's most corrupt elite. It will be the work of a generation to tax away their stolen loot, and much of it may never be recovered. These people will spend that time working to transform their wealth into permanent power, buying and installing politicians at every level of office.

Trumpland is a coalition of wreckers of every kind. Think of how MAHA undermined the nation's herd immunity to a host of communicable diseases, many of which can result in permanent disability. Long after MAHA is forgotten even as a punchline, the people whose health they destroyed forever will still be struggling. After a century of painstaking work to corral measles and other killer diseases, MAHA immunocompromised America itself, in just two short years. Any attempt to bring back evidence-based preventative medicine must now overcome the deep mistrust of medical science that an army of supplement-peddling quacks has sunk deep into Americans' psyche.

Speaking of mistrust: Americans must now and forever live with the knowledge that tens of thousands of their neighbors joined ICE, an armed, masked kidnapping squad that occupied US cities, murdering US citizens and noncitizens alike in the streets with impunity. Even if we try and imprison every one of those war criminals, it will take years and will shatter families and communities.

ICE proved that America is awash in small arms, but it's a different story when it comes to significant warfighting materiel. Trump's Iranian disaster used up the largest part of Pax Americana's arsenal of missiles and anti-missile interceptors. Putin doesn't need to convince Trump to cut off Ukraine's access to America's long-range arsenal. Trump shot his wad, and re-arming America is the work of decades, and it will cost billions, and it will require access to things America no longer knows how to make. Worse: the places where they do know how to make those things are no longer America's allies.

Can they be America's allies again? Well, sure, but only in a limited, Carneyist, "minilateral" way, in which countries form temporary alliances to accomplish specific goals. Biden spoke of "friendshoring" production of key goods and services. Friendshoring implies a reliable form of friendship, the sort that is built on decades of trust and interdependence. Friendshoring only works if the friends you friendshore to can be relied upon to stay your friends. Do we really think that if Venezuela deposes the puppet regime Trump installed after kidnapping the country's leader that it will remain America's "friend?"

That's the problem with weaponized interdependence: it only works for so long as the country America is screwing remains dependent on America, and now every country in the world is moving heaven and earth to break their dependencies on America, its institutions and products:
https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties

As Nate Bethea says on this week's Trashfuture podcast, airports outside of the USA are now filled with large, splashy ads urging businesses to move their IT out of America's cloud and off of American apps:
https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties

After Microsoft obliged the Trump regime by taking away the online accounts of foreign officials who made Trump angry, will any other country ever voluntarily trust them with their industrial capacity, let alone their government?
https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/

I'm not saying America is a write-off: I'm saying that it has been sabotaged down to the foundation slab and structural members by a psychotic cadre of skilled arsonists, who were abetted by mad bombers who drove themselves even crazier by racking up life-altering debts in rigged "prediction markets" that serve as a vehicle for bankrupting yourself by wishcasting away your life's savings by betting on every aspect of a Permanent Chud Reich, as corrupt officials make out like bandits by trading on insider information.

When America comes back (if America comes back), it will not be as the organizing platform for the world's finance, military, technology and commerce. In years or perhaps decades, America may find a new stable place in the international community. But in the meantime, it cannot be relied upon to serve as the world's hyperpower. Trump forever disqualified America from enjoying that privileged place – and just to be sure, he destroyed its capacity to even try.

America cannot undo Trumpism (permalink)

True Carneyism has never been tried. When Canadian PM Mark Carney traveled to Davos to declare a "rupture" in the old order (and admit that this old order was never that great to begin with) he told us that there was no going back from Trumpism. The only way out of Trumpism was through:
https://www.weforum.org/stories/forum-institutional/davos-2026-special-address-by-mark-carney-prime-minister-of-canada/
This is easy to say, but hard to do. If the old order is over, then we will never again be able to trust America to serve as the world's cop, banker, ISP, IT department and consumer of first resort.
We can't trust Americans to buy the things we make:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/16/k-shaped-recovery/#disenshittification-nations
We can't trust them not to interfere with the interconnections between fiber lines that slither out of the oceans and onto the US landmass:
https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/26/difficult-multipolarism/#eurostack
We can't trust them not to weaponize the US dollar to undermine sovereign nations' legitimate activities:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/26/i-dont-want/#your-greenback-dollar

And we absolutely can't trust them not to spy on, steal from, and shut down governments, firms and households around the world by cutting off access to US software and cloud services, and by bricking the world's devices, from tractors to smartphones:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

Despite Carney's assertion that this rupture represents a welcome (if too cruel, sudden and painful) departure of the old (never very good) system, no one (not even Carney) is acting like the world has truly changed. Take Carney's answer to the Trump tariffs: retaliatory tariffs. Tariffs have a place in sheltering a nascent domestic industry from better-developed, deeper-pocketed foreign competitors, so a tariff wall between Canada and the US could make sense, if it was paired with the massive domestic investment we'd need to rebuild the manufacturing industry that Brian Mulroney sold out with the Canada-US Free Trade Agreement (and later NAFTA).

But Carney is no Carneyist. When it comes to massive domestic spending, Carney is a bog-standard, austerity-addled Reaganomics guy; a central banker and technocrat whose idea of "industrial policy" is firing tens of thousands of skilled civil servants who thwart his agenda and replacing them with defective (but obedient) chatbots running on US hardware:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/13/vibe-governance/#k-hole

Carney's retaliatory tariffs aren't what you'd do if the old order had "ruptured." They're what you'd do if you hoped that your American cousins would come to their senses, evict their mad king from the White House, tear down the Epstein Memorial Ballroom, and roll back the clock to 2016. Like a lot of liberals, Carney just wants to go back to brunch.

But as any true Carneyist knows, brunch is canceled forever. Brunch ruptured. There's no going back to the old America, and there's no going back to the old American order that had dominated the world since the end of WWII. As November Kelly says, "Trump inherited a poker game rigged in his favor, but he flipped the table over anyway because he resented having to pretend to play."

This is something we're all struggling with, including Americans. The Republicans' midterm wipeout has corporate Democrats hoping that after a few years' tinkering, they can elect a Newsomdroid or give Harris a do-over and win back the trust and reliance of the world and the American people. Even for a true Carneyist who never liked the old order very much (like me), this is a comforting prospect. No one knows what the next world will look like, and no matter how screwed up the old world was, I knew how it worked and how to make it work for me (more or less).

But there is no going back. Trump I didn't have a plan, it only had Trump, whose One Big Idea was issuing Executive Orders. Many of these were meaningless bloviating. Some were illegal and were swiftly suspended or never went into effect. Biden overturned nearly all the remaining EOs (that were both substantive and not totally illegal).

But Trump II had Project 2025. The point of Project 2025 and the ambition of the wreckers who wrote it was to push America through a series of one-way transformations that cannot be undone, and that's what's happened, over two short years. That's the bad news. The good news is that it's much easier to destroy than to build, so Project 2025 hasn't led to the creation of permanent, load-bearing fascist institutions that cannot be shuttered without bringing down large parts of the USA.

Start with values. Trumpism is a denial of democracy and the rule of law. Tens of millions of Americans have been marinated in a belief system that says that the way to win power is to claim all the elections you lose are rigged and that these "stolen elections" are best addressed by staging a coup. These people are in a cult that embraces its leader's naked corruption. They're in a cult whose doctrine treats political triumph of as divine direction to embark on looting sprees. It's a cult whose members mutilate their faces so that they can't ever leave, and the reward for this permanent disfigurement is endless influence-peddling:
https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6136101-ambassador-guilfoyle-wire-request/

Even without ritual scarification to mark them out forever, millions of these people will never come back from this cult indoctrination. They will forever be democracy's enemies, treating the idea of laws, rules and honest service as shucks for the rubes. What's more, these people's neighbors, family members and co-workers will never be able to fully trust them.

Unfortunately, those values aren't just diffused through the population: they are concentrated in the organs of state. DOGE and Federalist Society judicial appointments have created a stay-behind cadre of life-tenured fascists who now dominate America's federal judiciary and permanent civil service, including and especially the nation's law enforcement and national security agencies, from the FBI to the FDA, the NSA to the Bureau of Prisons.

Worse: DOGE also chased away hundreds of thousands of skilled, principled public servants. Those people have retired, retrained, emigrated or exited the workforce. They can't simply be re-hired and restored to their old roles. From finance regulation to the national education system, America has lobotomized itself, swapping people who understand how things work and use that understanding to enforce the laws and safeguard the American people for end-times fascists, caliper-wielding eugenicists, and Ayn Rand LARPers.

Much of the work DOGE's victims did is also gone forever. When DOGE's muskrats killed long-running NIH research projects, they pulled the plug on studies, some of which had run for decades. Many of these experiments are unsalvageable. DOGE didn't just throw away the contributions that cancer patients, people with genetic disorders and other volunteer research subjects gave to science: in halting these research projects, DOGE shredded this selfless sacrifice. Why not? When one NIH official begged his DOGE invaders not to kill long-running, valuable cancer research, the DOGE child laughed and said it didn't matter, because AI was going to cure cancer.

Then there's the NIH's research partners: the elite institutions who buckled so quickly in the face of Trump's antisemitism/DEI witch-hunts. These universities now face the same crisis as the DOGE-gutted civil service, with their best and brightest gone, grad students chased back to their home countries, and the trust of their students and faculty permanently squandered.

It's not just grad students who got chased out of America. Immigrants – documented and undocumented alike – have been terrorized for two years and many of them have fled. ICE got what it wanted: they robbed aging, stagnant America of the dynamism, aspiration and youthful vigor of the most ambitious people from every corner of the globe, people who proved their resourcefulness and bravery by making dangerous crossings. Then they navigated the US immigration system's impenetrable bureaucracy, often working without legal representation, in a language they were just learning, and still managing to clear every bureaucratic hurdle. This alone is a breathtaking demonstration of intelligence, resourcefulness and diligence. Those brilliant, hardworking people aren't coming back: some other country will get the benefit of their life's work and care. Their children will become citizens of other nations.

Now think of the hundreds of billions of dollars that have been transferred from ordinary working people who are still here, to America's oligarchs. Trump's tax cuts, corrupt policy subsidies and no-bid pork contracts have supercharged the wealth (and thus the power) of America's most corrupt elite. It will be the work of a generation to tax away their stolen loot, and much of it may never be recovered. These people will spend that time working to transform their wealth into permanent power, buying and installing politicians at every level of office.

Trumpland is a coalition of wreckers of every kind. Think of how MAHA undermined the nation's herd immunity to a host of communicable diseases, many of which can result in permanent disability. Long after MAHA is forgotten even as a punchline, the people whose health they destroyed forever will still be struggling. After a century of painstaking work to corral measles and other killer diseases, MAHA immunocompromised America itself, in just two short years. Any attempt to bring back evidence-based preventative medicine must now overcome the deep mistrust of medical science that an army of supplement-peddling quacks has sunk deep into Americans' psyche.

Speaking of mistrust: Americans must now and forever live with the knowledge that tens of thousands of their neighbors joined ICE, an armed, masked kidnapping squad that occupied US cities, murdering US citizens and noncitizens alike in the streets with impunity. Even if we try and imprison every one of those war criminals, it will take years and will shatter families and communities.

ICE proved that America is awash in small arms, but it's a different story when it comes to significant warfighting materiel. Trump's Iranian disaster used up the largest part of Pax Americana's arsenal of missiles and anti-missile interceptors. Putin doesn't need to convince Trump to cut off Ukraine's access to America's long-range arsenal. Trump shot his wad, and re-arming America is the work of decades, and it will cost billions, and it will require access to things America no longer knows how to make. Worse: the places where they do know how to make those things are no longer America's allies.

Can they be America's allies again? Well, sure, but only in a limited, Carneyist, "minilateral" way, in which countries form temporary alliances to accomplish specific goals. Biden spoke of "friendshoring" production of key goods and services. Friendshoring implies a reliable form of friendship, the sort that is built on decades of trust and interdependence. Friendshoring only works if the friends you friendshore to can be relied upon to stay your friends. Do we really think that if Venezuela deposes the puppet regime Trump installed after kidnapping the country's leader that it will remain America's "friend?"

That's the problem with weaponized interdependence: it only works for so long as the country America is screwing remains dependent on America, and now every country in the world is moving heaven and earth to break their dependencies on America, its institutions and products:
https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties

As Nate Bethea says on this week's Trashfuture podcast, airports outside of the USA are now filled with large, splashy ads urging businesses to move their IT out of America's cloud and off of American apps:
https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties

After Microsoft obliged the Trump regime by taking away the online accounts of foreign officials who made Trump angry, will any other country ever voluntarily trust them with their industrial capacity, let alone their government?
https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/

I'm not saying America is a write-off: I'm saying that it has been sabotaged down to the foundation slab and structural members by a psychotic cadre of skilled arsonists, who were abetted by mad bombers who drove themselves even crazier by racking up life-altering debts in rigged "prediction markets" that serve as a vehicle for bankrupting yourself by wishcasting away your life's savings by betting on every aspect of a Permanent Chud Reich, as corrupt officials make out like bandits by trading on insider information.

When America comes back (if America comes back), it will not be as the organizing platform for the world's finance, military, technology and commerce. In years or perhaps decades, America may find a new stable place in the international community. But in the meantime, it cannot be relied upon to serve as the world's hyperpower. Trump forever disqualified America from enjoying that privileged place – and just to be sure, he destroyed its capacity to even try.

blocks.text: I cut bot traffic to my site by over 80% with a simple trap.

Last month, my hobby website OpenBenches.org transferred more than 2.5TB of data to visitors. As much as I'd like to think the site is enormously popular, it looks like it is just AI bots endlessly crawling the data and slurping up the images.
So I've built B6 to be an indiscriminate tool to eradicate these unwanted parasites.
It is very loosely inspired by Jeff Starr's Blackhole, but works even on sites with heavy caching.
Here's the high level description of how it works.

Create a directory like 
							/honeypot/
							 on your site

Put some code in 
							index.php
							 within the directory

Add the honeypot as an explicit "Disallow" in 
							robots.txt
Include a hidden link to to the honeypot on every page of your site

If something accesses that page, write its IP address to your 
							.htaccess

The 
							.htaccess
							 bans the IP address from ever accessing your site again.
This blog post shows you how you can build this yourself and discusses some of the problems it might cause.
Bad Robots!
The file robots.txt lives at the root of your website. It contains a list of instructions to automated web crawlers. Respectful bots will read it and refuse to look at specific parts of your site.
Add these two lines to it:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /honeypot/
That says bots shouldn't visit any page in the honeypot directory.
Bots generally check for updates every 24 hours, so either wait a day or manually submit it to major crawlers.
.htaccess
The .htaccess file contains a list of instructions for how your server should process requests.
Find the bit of your .htaccess file which looks like this:

<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
        RewriteEngine On
        RewriteBase /
Edit it to look like this:

<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
        RewriteEngine On
        RewriteBase /

### BLOCKED IPs
    #   TEST-NET-1
    RewriteCond %{REMOTE_ADDR} "=192.0.2.1"
    RewriteRule ^ - [R=402,L]
### /BLOCKED IPs
It is important that these rules come before any other rewrite rules.
Change the end of this IfModule to look like:

</IfModule>

ErrorDocument 402 "Payment Required - Access Denied."
If an IP address is in the blocked IP list, the server will send an error code and a readable message. You can add whatever plain text you like here.
Wipe Them All Out

Inside the honeypot directory, create a file called index.php (or whatever you like). When this page is visited, it grabs the visitor's IP address and the name of its User Agent. It then places them in the BLOCKED IPs section.
Setting The Trap
Web crawlers look at a page, find every link on it, then visit those links. So we need to put a link to the honeypot on every page - but in such a way that normal users will not find it or click it.
This adds a link, removes it from the accessibility tree, and gives it impossible to click text (a zero width joiner).
‍
This CSS hides it from normal viewers and removes the mouse cursor from view.
Problems This Might Cause
It's unlikely that a human will find the link, click on it, and be banned. But if they do, consider put a message in the blocking text telling them how they can get unblocked.

Some useful bots ignore robots.txt. If they identify themselves via a User-Agent string (and they should) you can manually remove them from .htaccess. You could also code in an allow list exemption for them. But, of course, many bad bots lie about who they really are.
Conversely, not all bots crawl every link. This won't catch bots which respect robots.txt but are nevertheless problematic.

If you have thousands of different bots blocked, the performance of your server might slow down while .htaccess is parsed. There's weak anecdotal evidence that it adds a slight overhead. But, personally, I don't think that's worth worrying about.

Bots often use hijacked IP addresses. After the bot has moved, an innocent party might be blocked from your site. Each block has a timestamp associated with it. You could periodically unblock older entries.
Bots rotate through hundreds of different IP addresses. So the same bot might get blocked multiple times.

Bots might see the CSS marks the link as hidden and refuse to follow it. Instead of CSS, you could use invisible spaces or other characters which would be hard for a human to see but appear visible to a bot.

Similarly, a smart bot might refuse to visit a path called /honeypot/ so choose a better name for it. A smarter bot would see that touching the honeypot leads to a ban - so perhaps a selection of traps are needed?

As is implied in the name, this is a blunt banhammer. It doesn't give a warning, nor does it look at User-Agent, Country, or any other signal. You touch the honeypot and you receive an instaban. No warning and no automated way to appeal.
Alternatives

There are alternative ways to do this. Some bots don't send language headers, some use older versions of HTTP, they often have severely outdated User Agent strings. Those are all reasonable ways to block something which is probably a bot. There are likely to be a few false positives though.
But B6 has no false positives. A normal user can't follow the link to the trap and a well-behaved bot won't follow the link.
Things like Anubis require a lot of work to set up and annoy normal users. B6 doesn't require a specific hosting environment and is never shown to normal users.
It Works!
Since running B6 a week ago, I've blocked over 400 IP addresses and seen a significant fall in traffic. I've not had any complaints yet. Sadly, none of the bots have paid to remove the paywall!
At peak, my site was seeing 216GB of data transfer per day. That's now dropped to around 25GB.

I don't claim this is the most sophisticated bot blocker in existence - but I enjoyed building it myself. I'll probably add something to records the geolocation of the IP and maybe remove any block older than a certain age.
If you'd like to use it or improve this code, I'd be grateful if you treated it as AGPL v3 licensed.

blocks.text: Steiner triples
Several examples from the recent posts on finite geometry are special cases of Steiner triples.
A Steiner triple system, written STS(n), is a set S of n elements and a collection of three-element subsets of S called blocks, such that every two-element subset of S belongs to exactly one block.
STS(7) is the smallest finite projective plane, the Fano plane, and STS(9) is the smallest finite affine plane. In both cases you interpret the elements of S as points and the blocks as lines.
Several questions come up naturally. First, for which values of n does an STS(n) exist? A necessary and sufficient condition for is that n = 1 or 3 mod 6.

For a given n, can there be more than one STS(n), i.e. are there Steiner triple systems of the same size that are not isomorphic? Yes indeed. The number of non-isomorphic instances grows rapidly with n.

When does (some instance of) STS(n) correspond to a projective or affine space? When n = 2k − 1 for k ≥ 3. For n ≥ 13 there are multiple isomorphism classes of STS(n), so for k > 3 there will be an instance of STS(2k − 1) that corresponds to a projective space and other instances that do not. The instance that does correspond to a projective plane will be isomorphic to a finite field analog of the real projective plane.

Steiner triple systems are a special case of Steiner systems. A Steiner system S(t, k, n) is a set of n items and a collection of blocks that are k-element subsets such that every set of t items belongs to a unique block. Steiner triples are S(2, 3, n) systems.

Steiner systems often correspond to finite geometries with the blocks interpreted as lines. As with the special case of triples, there can be non-isomorphic instances of Steiner systems, and so when I say below that S(t, k, n) corresponds to a certain geometry, I mean that at least one instance corresonds to that geometry.
Projective
The Steiner system
with q a prime power greater than 2 is a d-dimensional projective space.
Affine
The space
S(2, q, qd)
is an affine space. Again q > 2 is a prime power.
Hyperbolic

The finite hyperbolic plane given as an example in an earlier post corresponds to S(2, 2, 6). Many other Steiner systems are hyperbolic, but I’m not aware of a tidy classification similar to the ones above.
Steiner systems outside geometry

Steiner systems were named after Swiss mathematician Jakob Steiner because he published a highly cited article asking questions about what we now call Steiner triples. His interest in these systems was combinatorial. Others developed the connections to geometry later.
Steiner systems arise in several areas of mathematics outside of geometry, including coding theory, design of experiments, and graph theory.

blocks.text: Euclid’s fifth postulate says that given a line ℓ and a point P not on ℓ , there is a unique line through P parallel to ℓ. In the projective plane there are no parallel lines, and in the hyperbolic plane there are at least two lines through P parallel to ℓ.
Recent posts have looked at finite projective and affine planes. This post will look at finite hyperbolic planes.

Finite projective planes come up far more often in application than finite hyperbolic planes. I’ve seen several resources on finite geometries that don’t mention the hyperbolic case. Finite hyperbolic geometries have less structure than their projective or affine counterparts and so are less useful.
The definition of a finite hyperbolic plane isn’t entirely standardized. We will use the following axioms for this post.
Any two distinct points lie on exactly one line.
Given a line ℓ and a point P not on ℓ, there exist at least two lines through P parallel to ℓ.
There exist four points, no three collinear.
Every line contains at least two points.

An example of a system satisfying these axioms is the complete graph of six vertices. The nodes are the points and the edges are the lines. In set-theoretic terms, the points are the one-element subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and the lines are all possible two-element subsets.

Note that lines in the finite hyperbolic plane are two element sets. The lines {5, 6} and {1, 3}, for example, are parallel because they do not intersect, even though the representations of {5, 6} and {1, 3} in the visualization above are not parallel in the Euclidean sense.

There are many other examples of system satisfying the hyperbolic plane axioms. Too many in some sense. You could say finite hyperbolic systems are less common in application because they are more common in count.

There are many other examples of system satisfying the hyperbolic plane axioms. Too many in some sense. You could say finite hyperbolic systems are less common in application because they are more common in count.

blocks.text: The previous post was on finite projective planes. This post will look at finite affine planes and the next will look at finite hyperbolic planes.

Affine geometry is essentially what remains of Euclidean geometry if you keep the incidence properties, e.g. wanting to know whether things intersect, and forget about metric properties such as segment lengths and angle measurements. As with projective planes, affine planes can be finite.
The axioms of an affine plane are as follows.
Any two distinct points lie on exactly one line.
For any line ℓ and point P not on ℓ, there is exactly one line through P that doesn’t intersect ℓ.
There exist three points that are not collinear.
The second axiom says that affine geometry is Euclidean, or maybe Euclidean-lite. It lacks features of Euclidean geometry, but it doesn’t contradict Euclidean geometry.

To construct an example of a finite affine plane, let p be an odd prime and construct a p × p grid with x– and y-coordinates 0, 1, 2, …, p − 1. The affine lines are essentially the Euclidean lines that pass through the grid points, if lines can wrap around the sides, i.e. you’re working on a discrete torus. Algebraically, lines are the solutions to x = c and y = mx + b mod p.

A finite affine plane always has n² points and n² + n lines. The number n can be an odd prime, or any prime power greater than 2. It is unknown whether there are examples in which n is not a prime power. There are no affine planes of order 6 or 10, and the case of n = 12 is open.

We’re excited to announce Ninety, the first prediction market for open source security, launching today in partnership with Lanternfish, the frontier AI lab for software security. Security report volumes at major projects are four to five times higher than in 2024. Attackers and defenders are both running frontier models against the same few thousand packages, and everything those models turn up is scattered across disclosure inboxes, private chats, embargo lists and exploit brokers, with no price attached.

Ninety puts a price on it. Anyone can take a position on whether an open source project will have a vulnerability disclosed, how severe it will be, and how long the fix will take. Researchers earn from the markets they called correctly, and defenders who harden code earn when contracts resolve NO. Everyone who depends on open source gets a per-project price for how secure their dependencies are, updated every second.
Rationale

Bug bounties make one payment to whoever finds a bug, after the report is in. Grant programs fund a handful of projects a year after a long application process. Both fall behind when a single model run can produce forty plausible reports before lunch, and this year several bounties closed. curl ended its bug bounty in January and Google paused its open source VRP in October, citing “a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid.” HackerOne’s Internet Bug Bounty paused new submissions and cut its medium-severity payout from $1,843 to $297. Ninety replaces the submission queue with an order book, and every new report moves the price.

Writing about curl’s bug bounty in 2024, Daniel Stenberg called it “an absolute and undisputed success”. Ninety takes the same incentive and makes it continuous and open to anyone with a verified account.
Mechanics

Each market is a binary contract on a single project over a fixed window. The standard term is ninety days, matching the industry disclosure deadline and giving Ninety its name. Contracts trade between $0 and $1, and the price is the traders’ current estimate of the probability that the event happens. Launch markets include:
curl: Will a CVE rated High or Critical be published before 31 January 2027?
OpenSSL: Will the next major release ship before the next High-severity advisory?
Linux: Over/under on kernel CVEs published in December, line set by Lanternfish.
lodash: Will the maintainers respond to the next security report within 14 days?
PHP: Will a follow-up fix for php2shell be needed before 1 February 2027?

Every listed project also has a set of standard side markets: days-to-patch, whether a fix gets backported to older release lines, whether the advisory gets a name and a logo, and whether the repository is archived or its sole maintainer steps down before expiry.

Contracts can be chained into parlays, which pay out when every leg resolves YES, with odds set by Lanternfish. A dependency parlay has a leg for each step of a fix through the graph, such as a High-severity advisory in zlib followed by a CVE for each listed project that vendors it. The most popular parlay in beta was the Long Weekend, with legs for a Critical CVE published on a Friday, the first fix released after Monday, and the sole maintainer stepping down within the contract window.
Results

Ninety has been in private beta with a few hundred traders since the summer. The PHP “CVSS 9+ before Halloween” contract traded at four cents for most of September. It closed at 97 cents on the afternoon of 20 October, the day before PHP shipped fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and CISA’s addition of both to the KEV catalog on 26 October settled the follow-on exploitation contract. Congratulations to whoever was buying in September.

Our most traded contract of the year is the exploit count over/under on Copy Fail, the Linux kernel privilege escalation found with AI assistance in April. It resolved at 132 public proofs of concept.

Backtested against historical data, the 2024 xz-utils backdoor would have been the most profitable position in open source history. The account best placed to take it had commit access to the project and would have been barred under our insider rules.
“I used to send reports to maintainers and wait months for a reply,” said Max Tokens, the top-earning YES trader in the beta. “These days I buy YES on the project first and then file the report.”

“We run Lanternfish against every project we hold NO on, and the returns cover the compute,” said Ram Hoarder, who leads a four-person defensive trading desk on the NO side. “Patches go into our fork until the contract expires, which protects the position.”
Lanternfish

Ninety is sponsored by Lanternfish, whose models are used by most of the researchers who find open source vulnerabilities and most of the teams who fix them. Every verified trader gets Lanternfish credits on signup. Lanternfish is Ninety’s designated market maker and provides liquidity on both sides of every contract. On the Copy Fail over/under it made the market on both sides while traders using its models generated most of the 132 proofs of concept being counted. Each of those model runs counted toward the Security Investment Score of the trader who ran it, which tracks Lanternfish usage and is shown on their public profile next to their returns.

“Security in 2026 is a compute problem,” said Chip Shortage, CEO of Lanternfish. “Attackers are using frontier models to find bugs, so defenders have to use them too, and Ninety pays both sides back for the compute.”
Integrity

Ninety has strict insider rules to keep prices fair. Trading on a project is blocked for anyone with commit, release or publish access to it, anyone named in its maintainers file, code owners or security policy, and anyone who received an embargoed report about it in the last twelve months. We match identities against commit history, registry ownership records and signing keys automatically, so maintainers are excluded without signing up. “Maintainers are excluded the day their project is listed,” said Chuck Sum, Ninety’s Head of Market Integrity. “Most of them have no idea Ninety exists, which is exactly what you want from an insider control.”

A trader who opens a pull request against a listed project becomes an insider for that project when the pull request is opened, and their positions are closed at the current price. Most traders hold fixes in a private fork until their contracts expire.

Maintainers know more about their own projects than anyone else, so they’re the one group permanently excluded. We expect most of them to be fine with that. As Daniel Stenberg wrote earlier this year, “I am not in this game for the money or the extravagant life style.”

Traders may research the projects they hold positions in, including submitting security reports, requesting CVEs, opening issues, and asking for status updates on existing reports. Any contact with a maintainer intended to influence a market outcome must be disclosed on the trader’s profile within 24 hours.

Markets resolve when any CNA publishes a CVE record for the project, and resolution is based on publication alone. Records that are later disputed or rejected still resolve YES if they were published inside the contract window.
Listing

Any project with a package on a major registry and at least one CVE in its history is listed automatically. Ninety lists projects without asking their maintainers, because the security of widely used software is a matter of public interest and the markets reflect information that already exists.

Maintainers can request delisting from any market page. A delisting request is material non-public information about the project, so it’s disclosed to traders as soon as it’s received and marked on the price chart. Archiving a repository settles that project’s abandonment markets, and its other markets run to expiry.

0.1% of all trading fees go into the Maintainer Appreciation Pool, paid out quarterly to the maintainers of listed projects as Lanternfish credits, with the largest shares going to projects whose markets resolve NO most often. Credits can be spent on Lanternfish’s report triage models. Each listed project also gets one complimentary read-only dashboard seat, and maintainers can apply for delayed market data on their own projects, released ninety days after each contract settles.
Organisations

Teams can buy YES across their dependency tree as a hedge, so a critical CVE in a transitive dependency pays out when your exposure is highest, and for most organisations a hedged dependency tree costs less than a support contract. “We moved our open source sponsorship budget into a YES position across our whole dependency tree,” said Audrey Trail, CISO at a Fortune 100 retailer. “It’s paid out four times this year.”

Upload an SPDX or CycloneDX SBOM and Ninety builds the hedge for you. Each listed component gets its own YES contract. Teams now have a financial reason to update the SBOM whenever a dependency changes.

Since 11 September, manufacturers selling into the EU have had to report actively exploited vulnerabilities under the Cyber Resilience Act. The early warning is due within 24 hours. Ninety’s CRA hedge adds an exploitation contract for every component in your SBOM. Each position is sized to the Act’s maximum fine: €15 million or 2.5% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. When one of your dependencies is exploited, the payout arrives before your early warning is due.

The Ninety price feed is available to software composition analysis vendors as a per-package security signal, and procurement teams can set a minimum NO price for any dependency entering their software.
Availability
Ninety is live today in 41 jurisdictions. Sign up, verify your identity, and connect a Lanternfish key. Your first ten trades are free. Know the odds.
If you maintain a listed project, thank you for creating value for the Ninety ecosystem.

blocks.text: Recently, I took on a project that I thought would be a lot of fun … but in the end, I did not like how it made me feel. And I think it reflects the real dangers of leaning too aggressively on AI for stuff you’d like to try out.

A quick explainer: About four years ago, I got a hold of a JingPad, a Linux-based tablet with a massive Achilles’ heel. The problem? It was sold as a Linux-first tablet on ARM, but it was built around an SoC that was not actually particularly open. The Unisoc Tiger T510, as I’ve written, was built for Android, and it has PowerVR graphics that didn’t have an open-source driver. Worse, the company that made it disappeared off the face of the Earth just a handful of months after it first appeared.

The JingPad was a working, fully functional tablet that had been done dirty by its ownership and a bad engineering decision. It was a perfect candidate for the very kind of deconstruction project that has been taking the internet by storm in recent weeks.

So, my goal was this: Let’s see if I can use Claude, Deepseek, Xiaomi MiMo, and other LLMs to get this dang thing working in a modern version of Linux. Certain components, namely the proprietary GPU, might prove difficult, but using Ghidra, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA), and a willing-to-go-at-it LLM, it could take things down the road for me.
How hard could it be?
The good, and bad, of an insane yak-shaving project

This is an example of yak-shaving, a concept in which one project gradually evolves into numerous complex branches that never seem to end. For those not familiar, it is based on a Ren & Stimpy skit called “Yak Shaving Day,” which I’ve helpfully embedded above.
Tech projects have a tendency to devolve into wild goose chases like this, as hinted above, but this was a whole new beast to me.

Anyway, I want to make clear that this project wasn’t an outright failure. From literally nothing but an empty boot screen, we got the device to load a relatively modern version of Fedora on a “dirty” Linux kernel, based on 6.18. In many ways, it worked, complete with a working touchscreen screen, a charging battery, WiFi access, and an accessible GNOME interface. While not especially fast, I believe it is about as stable as JingOS, the software that came on it in 2022 and itself did not have GPU accelerated graphics.

There were even fun quirks that emerged as I was working on this. I got the flashlight for the camera working on the back, even though there’s literally no use case where it’d actually be useful. And I made significant progress adding FM radio support for the device, despite the fact that, like most mobile devices, FM radio support was never an actual feature of the tool. (In both cases, I thought it would be funny, even though the joke was honestly limited to just me.)

Unfortunately, getting to this point created a project that I would best describe as all-consuming. I had a swarm of different agents going at different components, different parts of the device, attempting to scrape details from old firmware versions and related projects in the hope that it’d uncover something missed previously. The result: I had to baby the damn thing all day, managing a bunch of LLMs and rebooting the device as the agents I was using went down one dead-end after another. And shockingly, the thing that kind of made the process less fun and more of a quagmire? It wasn’t the GPU, as I expected; it was the sound.

I got as far as having all the components of the sound card separately working; the DMA chip, the speakers, the codecs, and so on. The GNOME settings app even recognized that the sound card was there. But after receiving something like 50 “this is the last thing before you finally hear sound” messages from DeepSeek, I realized that I had gotten my own brain into a dangerous loop. It was nonstop dopamine hit on top of nonstop dopamine hit—the promise of instant gratification without getting gratified—and after a while, I kind of just felt mentally drained by it all.
This was a “me” project, one that I wanted to see in the world, but in the end it was kind of getting in the way of me thinking about literally anything else.

The way I broke the chain, at least for now, was simple: I put the tablet away for now. I’m going to try my best to get a healthy distance from it. If and when I come back to this project, I want to ensure I’m doing it for reasons that help me learn something rather than stress me out.
In the right context, things like this can be good

This all sounds like a dangerous hobby. But to make the counterargument: For years, we’ve heard stories about smart devices and other objects losing support over time because a company shut down a server somewhere, or chose not to modernize them. With moves like these, we can revive these devices.

For example, the seemingly dead Hackintosh scene has actually seen signs of life, thanks to AI. There’s now a driver for modern-day Nvidia cards on Intel Hackintoshes. It is now possible to boot MacOS on a Snapdragon PC. And Cutefish, a new MacOS-like distro, has promised something previously thought impossible—working graphical MacOS apps in a Linux environment.
A decade ago, when Hackintosh was hitting its peak point in popularity, all this stuff was crazy talk. No way was this going to happen.

And to be clear, there have been other projects I’ve tried that went way better than the one above. As I recently wrote in Boxed News, I was able to turn Dux Shell (formerly Dank Material Shell) into a usable TV computing experience.

Yes, AI is capable of reshaping computing experiences in new ways, in ways that some might find culturally frustrating if the reason you get into tech is because of specific scenes. (I personally don’t, and think the line between cool stuff and gatekeeping is quite small.)

But I’m personally of the view that in cases like the JingPad, where this tablet would be sitting around being useless otherwise, stuff like REA could have genuine value. After all, even if I don’t end up using it to type the next Great American blog post, it can still be useful as a makeshift self-hosting device or even just a lightweight way to surf the web. And I’m hopeful that, eventually, I’ll turn this into a feature-complete device, even with the components that Unisoc and Imagination didn’t bother to make public. However …
Shave yaks? If you value your mental health, pace yourself

If there’s anything I’ve learned about myself over the past decade, I get sucked into different directions way too easily. I can get obsessed with things, and that obsession can sometimes lead to cool places. (See &udm=14.)

But something about the process of attempting to use AI to fix an old tablet felt kind of damaging to a routine in a way that few of my hobbies have over the years. I mentioned Hackintoshing before, and honestly that’s kind of what it reminds me of the most, this attempt to make something do a thing it was never meant to do. But when so much of what you’re doing is working up against something hyping up every action, it’s hard not to feel hollow at the end of it.

As is highlighted by the fact that I publish a little less often these days, I don’t use AI for any of my actual writing. I try taking my time with it. But in a world where it seems like AI is the decorative bird of technology, it can intrude in dangerous ways, with costs that don’t necessarily show themselves right away. And I’m not talking about tokens.

I’m a well-known yak shaver. It’s what I do. This newsletter is a shrine to yak-shaving at the end of the day. But I did not like the way I felt at the end of this week, having hit the reset button on the JingPad for the 250th time. I’m sure I’m not alone here.

My suggestion to anyone else who yak-shaves: Approach agents with caution. After all, an AI agent does not have a limit; you do. Projects like these only take and take your energy, and leave you with a broken-feeling brain.
And unlike a static code window or a page of docs, an agent can make false claims or hype up promises it can’t back up.
