It was nonstop dopamine hit on top of nonstop dopamine hit—the promise of instant gratification without getting gratified—and after a while, I kind of just felt mentally drained by it all.
This was a “me” project, one that I wanted to see in the world, but in the end it was kind of getting in the way of me thinking about literally anything else.

The way I broke the chain, at least for now, was simple: I put the tablet away for now. I’m going to try my best to get a healthy distance from it. If and when I come back to this project, I want to ensure I’m doing it for reasons that help me learn something rather than stress me out.
In the right context, things like this can be good

This all sounds like a dangerous hobby. But to make the counterargument: For years, we’ve heard stories about smart devices and other objects losing support over time because a company shut down a server somewhere, or chose not to modernize them. With moves like these, we can revive these devices.

For example, the seemingly dead Hackintosh scene has actually seen signs of life, thanks to AI. There’s now a driver for modern-day Nvidia cards on Intel Hackintoshes. It is now possible to boot MacOS on a Snapdragon PC. And Cutefish, a new MacOS-like distro, has promised something previously thought impossible—working graphical MacOS apps in a Linux environment.
A decade ago, when Hackintosh was hitting its peak point in popularity, all this stuff was crazy talk. No way was this going to happen.

And to be clear, there have been other projects I’ve tried that went way better than the one above. As I recently wrote in Boxed News, I was able to turn Dux Shell (formerly Dank Material Shell) into a usable TV computing experience.

Yes, AI is capable of reshaping computing experiences in new ways, in ways that some might find culturally frustrating if the reason you get into tech is because of specific scenes. (I personally don’t, and think the line between cool stuff and gatekeeping is quite small.)

But I’m personally of the view that in cases like the JingPad, where this tablet would be sitting around being useless otherwise, stuff like REA could have genuine value. After all, even if I don’t end up using it to type the next Great American blog post, it can still be useful as a makeshift self-hosting device or even just a lightweight way to surf the web. And I’m hopeful that, eventually, I’ll turn this into a feature-complete device, even with the components that Unisoc and Imagination didn’t bother to make public. However …
Shave yaks? If you value your mental health, pace yourself

If there’s anything I’ve learned about myself over the past decade, I get sucked into different directions way too easily. I can get obsessed with things, and that obsession can sometimes lead to cool places. (See &udm=14.)

But something about the process of attempting to use AI to fix an old tablet felt kind of damaging to a routine in a way that few of my hobbies have over the years. I mentioned Hackintoshing before, and honestly that’s kind of what it reminds me of the most, this attempt to make something do a thing it was never meant to do. But when so much of what you’re doing is working up against something hyping up every action, it’s hard not to feel hollow at the end of it.

As is highlighted by the fact that I publish a little less often these days, I don’t use AI for any of my actual writing. I try taking my time with it. But in a world where it seems like AI is the decorative bird of technology, it can intrude in dangerous ways, with costs that don’t necessarily show themselves right away. And I’m not talking about tokens.

I’m a well-known yak shaver. It’s what I do. This newsletter is a shrine to yak-shaving at the end of the day. But I did not like the way I felt at the end of this week, having hit the reset button on the JingPad for the 250th time. I’m sure I’m not alone here.

My suggestion to anyone else who yak-shaves: Approach agents with caution. After all, an AI agent does not have a limit; you do. Projects like these only take and take your energy, and leave you with a broken-feeling brain.
And unlike a static code window or a page of docs, an agent can make false claims or hype up promises it can’t back up.

blocks.text: Radio Shack billed itself as “The Technology Store.” And at one time it was a consumer electronics giant. At its peak, it had more than 5,000 locations strategically placed so that a ridiculously high number of US citizens, possibly as high as 80 percent, lived within 10 minutes of one. This blog post collects and organizes everything I’ve written about this not-quite-gone, and definitely not forgotten icon.
History of Radio Shack and Tandy Corporation

Tandy Leather was founded in 1919 as a leather supply store owned by David Tandy and Norton Hinckley. Charles Tandy, one of David Tandy’s sons, took over the company in 1961. The company expanded greatly during the 1950s after the younger Tandy returned from serving in World War II.

Radio Shack was founded in 1921 by Theodore Deutschmann, a British immigrant, selling electronics components by retail and mail order. It took its name from the wooden structure on ships that housed their radio equipment. But by 1963, the chain was struggling and its creditors were looking for a way out. One of its creditors knew Charles Tandy and convinced him to look into the electronics retailer.
On April 1, 1963, Charles Tandy introduced himself to Radio Shack employees at the Ritz-Carlton in Boston. “I’m Charles Tandy from Fort Worth, Texas,” he said to the group. “I now own Radio Shack.”
Charles Tandy | How Tandy bought Radio Shack | Tandy Corporation’s IPO-less IPO (coming soon)
The Technology Store

Radio Shack billed itself as The Technology Store. In turning it around, Tandy aggressively closed underperforming stores and opened new ones. He preferred short-term leases to maintain flexibility to close or relocate stores as needed. Radio Shack stores became a fixture in malls and strip malls nationwide.

As consumers became more interested in electronics, computers, robots, and other things state of the art, Radio Shack was there to sell them what they needed, often under its own private label brands. When the PBS TV series Nova ran an episode in 1990 about Clifford Stoll, a Unix administrator who caught and uncovered an East German hacking ring, he recounted building a trap for them using parts he bought from Radio Shack.
1980s Technology | When Nova introduced hacking to the mainstream
Computers

Radio Shack was one of the first companies to sell prebuilt computers in 1977. Tandy didn’t know how many units it could sell. Management compromised on 5,000 units. They figured the stores could use unsold units for bookkeeping, and Charles Tandy thought the publicity from launching a computer would pay for the cost of developing the product and building 5,00 units. The initial production run sold out quickly and they soon had a waiting list.

It soon expanded into a full line of very successful computers with a dedicated following. The first computer magazine to specialize in a specific brand was 80micro, dedicated to Radio Shack TRS-80 computers.

Tandy/Radio Shack shifted to IBM compatible computers in 1983, a move that some in the industry mourned, because their computers had been relatively innovative. They provided a good balance of innovation, reliability, and price in addition to ready availability at thousands of stores nationwide.

Tandy 1000

The Tandy 1000 was Radio Shack’s most successful computer line, combining the improved graphics and sound of the IBM PCjr with better overall PC compatibility. Publishers like Sierra repackaged their PCjr titles as Tandy 1000 titles, sold them in Radio Shack stores, and Tandy priced the computers aggressively, bundling a monitor for free or running other specials. The critics had mixed opinions on it but the Tandy 1000 became the best selling computer in the United States.
It retains a following to this day.

Tandy monitors

Tandy sold several monitors for the Tandy 1000. Some of them were better than others, though they were generally reliable. If you like having a matched set, a matching monitor is a nice way to finish off your Tandy 1000. The CM-5 was inexpensive, so Tandy often bundled it with a computer when running a sale. It’s the most common model but it had some limitations.
Tandy CM-5 | Tandy CM-11 | Tandy 1000EX/HX monitor stand
Radio Shack toys

The wall of discrete electronic components made Radio Shack famous. But Charles Tandy quickly saw 80% of Radio Shack’s revenue came from 20% of its products. Tandy aggressively experimented with the 80% that wasn’t selling, rotating products out in search of new bestsellers.

Its toys were an excellent example of that. And not every toy Radio Shack sold was electronic, though the majority were. Radio Shack was The Technology Store, after all. Some of its toys were licensed from overseas manufacturers. Others were private-label knockoffs of popular toys that sold well in other stores.
Radio Shack Armatron | Radio Shack Fire Chief’s helmet | Radio Shack Hot Shot train | A Commodore 64-based Hummer TV game
Radio Shack’s decline and bankruptcy

Radio Shack went bankrupt in 2015, but it was a long time coming. I blogged about its decline over the years as it happened. That’s one advantage to blogging more than 20 years, I guess. It puts you in a position to capture a few things as they happened that in retrospect ended up being significant. And you can capture the mood at the time. My last visit to a Radio Shack physical location in 2016 felt like saying goodbye to a friend who seemed to not have much time left.

Today, one of its largest franchise operators now owns the whole brand. Radio Shack is never going to be what it once was, but I’m very glad the current owners have been able to salvage something from the brand and are selling Radio Shack-branded merchandise again. My slightly modernized Tandy 1000 reads its media from a modern Radio Shack-branded USB flash drive and sports a modern Radio Shack mouse pad. If you need an inexpensive gift idea for a retro computer enthusiast, some Radio Shack merch is a safe, easy bet.

But I do miss having a Radio Shack less than 10 minutes away with a good stock of batteries and cables and adapters and a reasonable stock of random electronics supplies. Batteries Plus just doesn’t have the same vibe Radio Shack had in its prime.
